paras: This clay tablet is about three thousand, four hundred years old. It spent more than three thousand years buried in the ruins of a lost city. And written on it... is the oldest song ever found.
Not a poem about music. Not a painting of a musician. An actual song. The words, and the instructions for how to play it.
So how did it survive? Who wrote it? And what did it actually sound like? Stick around, because by the end of this video, you're going to hear it.
I'm MJ, and this is MJ Sound Chronicles. The stories behind the sounds.

Our story starts in nineteen twenty-eight, on the coast of Syria. A farmer is plowing his field near a little hill called Rahs Shahmra... when his plow hits a stone. Underneath it, he finds an ancient tomb.
Archaeologists rush in. And under that hill, they find something much bigger than a tomb. They find a lost city. Its name was Oogareet.

Three thousand, four hundred years ago, Oogareet was one of the busiest port cities in the world. Ships came in from Egypt, from Cyprus, and from the Hittite empire in what is now Turkey. Tin, fish, pottery, timber. Everything passed through its harbor. And everything was written down... on clay.
The scribes of Oogareet wrote in cuneiform. Little wedge-shaped marks, pressed into wet clay with a reed.

Then, around eleven eighty-five B.C., it all came crashing down. Drought. Famine. Raiders from the sea. Letters from the city's final days beg for help that never came. Oogareet burned, and it was never rebuilt.

But here's the twist. Clay tablets are fragile. Leave them in the rain, and they melt back into mud. When the city burned, the fire baked many of its tablets hard, like pottery in a kiln. The disaster that destroyed the city... is the reason we can still read it.

Fast forward to the nineteen fifties. Digging through the ruins of the royal palace, French archaeologists pull out pieces of clay tablets covered in strange markings. Pieces of about thirty-six hymns. Almost all of them are broken beyond repair.
Except one. Three fragments that fit together into one nearly complete tablet. Scholars gave it a very boring name. H six. Hurrian Hymn number six.
Here's what makes it special. Across the top are the lyrics, written in Hurrian, the language of the Hurrian people. Then comes a double line. And underneath that... the music.

But it's not notes like we use today. It's a list of names for pairs of strings, each one followed by a number. Something like... kahbleeteh, three. Eerbooteh, one. Sahree, one. It's basically an ancient guitar tab.
And at the very bottom, the scribe signed his work. His name was Ahmoorahbee. He even wrote down which tuning to use.

And the instrument? A nine-stringed lyre, called a sammoom. Picture a small wooden frame with a crossbar, and strings you pluck by hand. The singer sings the words, and the lyre plays those pairs of strings underneath.
So who was the song for? A goddess named Nikkal. Goddess of orchards, and wife of the moon god. The lyrics seem to be about bringing her offerings. Some call it a love song. Others call it a prayer.
Honestly, the Hurrian language is so poorly understood that nobody can translate it fully. There are gaps where little flakes of clay have broken off.
Let's put its age in perspective. When this song was written, around fourteen hundred B.C., the pyramids of Giza were already more than a thousand years old.

It's about a thousand years older than the famous songs of ancient Greece, like the Seikilos epitaph, which is often called the oldest complete song. Between that scribe and you, there are more than a hundred generations of grandparents.
Now here's the catch. Scholars have argued about how to read this tablet for more than fifty years.

In the nineteen seventies, Anne Kilmer at Berkeley and Marcelle Duchesne-Guillemin worked out how the tablets describe tuning a lyre. And in nineteen seventy-four, the hymn was performed for the first time in modern history.

Since then, there have been at least five different interpretations. And each one sounds completely different. Some early versions even read the scale upside down, so the highest notes came out as the lowest!
And those numbers? Play the pair three times? Hold it for three beats? Nobody knows for sure.

So here's our own take. It's not a reconstruction, just a tribute. A nine-string lyre, an ancient seven-note scale, and pairs of strings played together, the way the tablet's instructions work. Close your eyes. Imagine a palace by the sea, three thousand, four hundred years ago. And listen.
Think about that. Empires rose and fell. The city burned. The language was forgotten. But a song survived, because someone, thirty-four centuries ago, decided it was worth writing down.
Music is older than writing. Older than cities. Maybe as old as people. And that's the story we're chasing on this channel.
